# Derbi Senda 50cc: Diagnosing Low Compression After a Top-End Swap

If you have recently rebuilt a Derbi Senda SM 50 from the 2005 era and are staring at zero compression readings despite fresh gaskets and a new top end, the issue likely isn't a mystery. You have installed the parts, but the assembly is not sealing correctly or the geometry is compromised. The fact that the engine sparks reliably indicates your ignition system (coils, CDI, spark plugs) is functioning as intended, so we can immediately rule out electrical failures in favor of mechanical integrity.

The symptom of "running only when bump started" before dying is a classic indicator of an engine that cannot sustain combustion due to insufficient air/fuel mixture pressure in the cylinder. When you kick or push-start the bike, you force enough air into the cylinder to allow ignition, but as soon as the throttle opens and the piston begins its upward stroke on the compression cycle, the lack of seal causes the pressure to drop below the threshold needed for stable combustion.

### Evaluating Piston Ring Fitment

When replacing a top end on a Derbi Senda, the most common failure point is the piston ring set. These 50cc two-stroke engines rely on specific ring gaps and tension to manage blow-by and maintain compression. If you sourced rings that were not specifically matched to this model year or if the rings are slightly out of specification, they will not seat properly into the cylinder wall grooves.

Verify that the ring gap is correct for your specific cylinder bore diameter. A gap that is too large allows combustion gases to escape directly into the crankcase, killing compression. Conversely, a gap that is too small can cause the rings to bind during thermal expansion, leading to scuffing and eventual seizure. Ensure the rings are fully seated in their grooves before reassembly; if they are not expanded to their full width during installation, they may sit partially outside the cylinder bore, creating a massive leak path immediately upon startup.

### Cylinder Bore Condition and Honing

Even with new gaskets and rings, the condition of the cylinder bore is critical. If the original cylinder was scored, out of round, or had an incorrect surface finish, new rings will not form a proper seal. A visual inspection using a borescope can reveal deep scratches or ovality that machining cannot fix without boring out the barrel.

If you did not hone the cylinder after installing new piston rings, the surface may still be rough enough to allow high-pressure gas to leak past the rings. Honing creates cross-hatching that helps retain oil and provides an initial sealing surface for the rings. Without this step, or if honing was done incorrectly, the engine will behave exactly as you described: difficult to start under load but able to run briefly with forced air intake.

### Valve Timing and Gasket Orientation

The head gasket on a Derbi Senda is not just a flat sheet; it often contains specific valve guide seals or integrated O-rings for the crankcase. If the gasket was installed backward, or if the valve seats were not honed to match the new valves, compression will be lost instantly upon combustion.

Check that the exhaust and intake ports are aligned correctly with the cylinder bore. Any misalignment can cause the piston to strike the port wall or prevent the valve from seating fully against the head surface. Additionally, ensure that the cam chain tensioner is properly adjusted. On these engines, excessive chain slack can push the timing gears out of alignment, causing the valves to open at the wrong time relative to the piston position. If a valve opens while the piston is compressing the mixture, the pressure bleeds straight into the crankcase, resulting in near-zero compression readings.

### Final Verification Steps

Before concluding that the engine is beyond repair, perform a leak-down test using compressed air introduced through the spark plug hole. Listen closely for hissing sounds at the intake, exhaust, or crankcase seals. If air escapes from the exhaust port when the piston is at Top Dead Center (TDC) on the compression stroke, the valve timing is off or the exhaust valve is not sealing.

If the cylinder bore is out of round by more than 0.1mm or the surface finish is poor, a simple top-end swap will not resolve the issue. You may need to machine the cylinder or replace it entirely with a new barrel to restore proper compression geometry.
